title: Image and likeness of God in the whole human; natural and supernatural
pass_a_gloss: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): although in ye man it is more illustrious — but ye image belonging toward God exists not in ye man only but also in ye woman. so that it be ye temple belonging toward ye Holy Spirit — in which not only ye soul but ye whole human plus even ye body itself is so restored — which is clear even out from ye restoration belonging toward this image. therefore ye whole human is rightly said to have been created toward ye image belonging toward God. but we do not altogether exclude ye human body out from ye reason belonging toward this image. most beautifully adorned with ye gifts belonging toward justice, holiness, plus truth — but we assert that its subject first plus through itself is ye rational soul. ye image belonging toward God is beheld in no visible thing except in humankind — in ye latter acceptance. only Christ can be called ye image belonging toward God — in ye former acceptance. or that which is made toward another — it signifies either ye archetype itself toward whose exemplar another is made. ye voice belonging toward image. Genesis 1:27; 5:1 — among some likeness is ye exegesis belonging toward image as if it were said ye most similar image belonging toward God. image indeed differs out from likeness as species out from genus. in which his highest perfection is beheld — that ye whole both by soul plus by body was created toward ye image belonging toward God plus according toward His likeness. there follows ye affection belonging toward humankind which is.
pass_b_english: There follows the affection of humankind, which is that the whole human, both by soul and by body, was created according to the image of God and after His likeness, in which his highest perfection is beheld. Image differs from likeness as species from genus; among some, likeness is the exegesis of image, as if it were said the most similar image of God — Genesis 1:27; 5:1.

The word image signifies either the archetype itself to whose exemplar another is made, or that which is made toward another. In the former acceptance only Christ can be called the image of God; in the latter, the image of God is beheld in no visible thing except in humankind. We assert that its subject first and through itself is the rational soul, most beautifully adorned with the gifts of justice, holiness, and truth. Yet we do not altogether exclude the human body from the reason of this image. Rightly, therefore, the whole human is said to have been created according to the image of God — which is clear even from the restoration of this image, in which not only the soul but the whole human, and even the body itself, is so restored as to be the temple of the Holy Spirit. And the image of God exists not in the man only but also in the woman, though in the man it is more illustrious.
source_text: Sequitur hominis affectio, quae est quod totus et anima et corpore conditus est ad imaginem Dei et secundum similitudinem ejus, in quo summa ejus perfectio conspicitur. Differt quidem imago a similitudine ut species a genere; apud quosdam similitudo exegesis imaginis est, quasi dicatur imago Dei simillima — Gen. I.27; V.1. Vox imaginis significat vel ipsum ἀρχέτυπον ad cujus exemplar aliud fit, vel id quod ad aliud fit. Priore acceptione solus Christus imago Dei dici potest; posteriore in nulla re aspectabili praeterquam in homine imago Dei conspicitur. Nos vero asserimus subjectum illius primo ac per se esse animam rationalem, justitiae sanctitatis ac veritatis donis pulcherrime exornatam. Corpus vero humanum ab imaginis hujus ratione non prorsus excludimus. Recte igitur dicitur totus homo ad imaginem Dei conditus — id quod vel ex instauratione hujus imaginis liquet, in qua non tantum anima sed totus homo ipsumque adeo corpus ita instauratur ut sit templum Spiritus Sancti. Imago autem Dei non in viro tantum sed et in femina exstat, licet in viro sit illustrior.
